transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. I'm Dr. [Name]. Can you tell me what brings you in today?

Um, yeah… I guess I came in because I keep getting really stuck on this one little uneven spot around my nose and cheek. It’s mostly in photos, or like under the bright lights at the store where I work, and then I can’t stop noticing it.

People tell me they don’t see anything, but it feels like it’s obvious, like customers or my managers are noticing it right away. I know that probably sounds small. The store lights are terrible anyway—like they make everyone look weird, and we just got these new ones near the registers—but for me it’s like that’s all I can focus on.
Do you find yourself spending a lot of time thinking about this uneven spot, even when you're not looking at photos or under bright lights?

Yeah… I do, kind of. I mean, it starts with seeing it in a photo or under the lights at work, but then it sticks in my head after. Like I’ll be ringing someone up and thinking they’re probably looking right at that spot near my nose and cheek.

And it’s frustrating because people say they don’t even notice it, and I’ll try to believe them, but then I remember how it looked in the store lighting—those lights honestly make everything look harsh—and I just keep thinking it must be the first thing customers or my manager sees.
Do you find yourself doing anything repeatedly—like checking mirrors, touching your face, or trying to cover that area—because of how you feel about that spot near your nose and cheek?

Yeah… I do. On my breaks I’ll go into the bathroom and check it in the mirror, like from different angles, and then I’ll mess with my hair to try to make it sit around that side of my face better.

It’s kind of embarrassing because sometimes I’m supposed to just be grabbing water or whatever, and then I’m still in there fixing it. And then, like, if girls come through my line with really smooth skin or just… normal faces, I end up comparing myself, which I know isn’t helpful. A couple times I’ve taken too long and been late getting back to the register.
Does this concern about the spot near your nose and cheek cause you a lot of distress, or make it hard for you to do things like work, socialize, or enjoy your daily activities?

Yeah… it does, mostly at work. Like, I don’t think I’m completely falling apart or anything, but my manager has noticed I’m coming back from breaks late, and I’m slower at the register sometimes because I get distracted.

And that stresses me out because I’m trying to get promoted, and I already feel like people at work judge every little thing. Like even the other day someone was talking about scheduling stuff and I thought, “Great, now they probably think I’m unreliable,” which—sorry, I know that’s not exactly what you asked. But yeah, it’s making work harder, and I’m worried it’s messing up how they see me.
Can you tell me more about how the spot near your nose and cheek looks to you? Do you feel like it's something that others should be able to see, even if they say they don't notice it?

It looks… like this little uneven patch, like around where my nose meets my cheek, and in certain photos it’s all I can see. Under the store lights it looks worse, like the texture or shadow just jumps out.

And yeah, even when people say they don’t see it, I kind of don’t believe them. Not like they’re lying exactly, but I feel like… how could they not? I’ll be at the register and someone will look at me and I’m thinking, they’re noticing that spot first.

Sorry, I keep talking about the store lights, but that’s honestly when it feels the most obvious. Like customers and managers must be able to see it, even if they say they don’t.
Outside of work or taking photos, do you find yourself thinking about this spot on your face for hours each day, to the point where it's hard to focus on other things?

Yeah… I mean, outside of work or pictures, it still kind of sticks in my head. Like I’ll be trying to watch something or do whatever at home and then I’ll remember that tiny uneven spot by my nose and cheek, and I start wondering if it looked bad earlier.

It’s not like I’m trying to think about it, it just keeps coming back. And then I think about the store lights, even when I’m not there, because they make it look so obvious to me. I know people say they don’t see it, but it feels like it has to be the first thing customers or managers notice when they look at me.

Sorry, I know you asked about hours… I don’t always count it exactly. It’s just a lot more than I want it to be, and it makes it hard to stay on whatever I’m supposed to be doing.
Is it mainly the thought of others noticing that spot that bothers you, or is it more about how that part of your face looks to you, regardless of what others might think?

I think it’s both, but… mostly it starts with how it looks to me. Like I get stuck on that tiny uneven spot around my nose and cheek, especially in photos or under the store lights, and then my brain jumps to, “Everyone else has to be seeing it too.”

Like customers, managers—especially managers, because I’m already trying to seem put together at work. Sorry, that’s kind of a work thing again. But even when people say they don’t notice it, I still feel like it’s the first thing they see when they look at me.
Do you find yourself doing things like checking your skin in the mirror, comparing your face to others, or trying to cover up that area repeatedly throughout the day?

Yeah… I do. Like on my breaks at work, I’ll go into the bathroom and check it in the mirror, and then I’ll try to fix my hair so it kind of falls around that side. Not always in a super obvious way, but I’m definitely doing it because of that spot.

And I compare myself to other girls who come through my line too, which sounds stupid when I say it. Like I’ll notice their skin looks normal or smooth, and then I’m thinking about mine again instead of just ringing people up.

Sometimes I take too long in the bathroom doing that stuff and then I’m late getting back to the register, and I have to act like I just lost track of time or something.

latest_inference.note: The patient's preoccupation with a perceived defect in their appearance, specifically around the nose and cheek, along with repetitive behaviors such as mirror checking, comparing themselves to others, and attempts to camouflage the area, strongly supports a diagnosis of Body Dysmorphic Disorder (F45.22). There is no clear evidence to support Social Anxiety Disorder (F40.24) as the primary concern appears to be about perceived physical appearance rather than fear of social scrutiny or evaluation.
